Nagle, 1984: batch tiny packets. Nagle's algorithm. Your client sends each request in two writes: first the headers, then the body. The headers go out immediately. author: Arjay McCandless
title: Why Simple Modulo Hashing Breaks Distributed Caches and How Consistent Hashing Solves It
summary: Using simple modulo hashing to distribute cache keys across servers causes widespread key remapping when adding or removing nodes, leading to cache stampedes and database overload. Consistent hashing avoids this by mapping servers and keys to a ring topology, ensuring that scaling the cache cluster only relocates a small subset of keys. This technique preserves hit rates and protects downstream databases during horizontal scaling.
transcript: Dude, this is really bad. I just added another cache server and our database is melting down. Okay, walk me through exactly what happened. We had three cache servers sitting in front of our database which were distributing the load fairly well. Cache utilization hit about 80%, so I figured we should add another cache server to reduce the load. Makes sense to me. What happened next? The second I added another cache server to help handle some of that load, our cache hit rate plummeted. It started sending all the requests straight to the database, and our database got overloaded. Wait, how were you deciding which cache server stores each key? We just take a hash of the key mod 4 to make sure the traffic is evenly distributed across all our cache servers. hash(key) % 4. There's your problem. Going from 3 to 4 servers can remap about 75% of your keys. Those requests will hit the wrong cache, miss, and then fall straight through to your database, causing the overload. Okay, that makes sense, but what should we do instead? You could fix this with consistent hashing. Instead of doing modulo by the number of servers, imagine every possible hash arranged around a ring. Then we hash each cache server onto that same ring. When a request comes in, we hash by its key, find that point on the ring, and then move clockwise until we hit a cache server, and that server owns that key. Then, when we add another server, we put that new server somewhere on the ring, and instead of redistributing almost every key, only the keys in that section of the ring move to the new server. The rest of the keys keep going to the same exact cache servers they were using before. How can I practice this stuff? You can study consistent hashing and other advanced system design concepts on my app, Devmaxx.
caption:
How to add a cache server safely
Consistent hashing is a way to distribute data across multiple servers without reshuffling almost everything every time you add or remove one.
With a simple hash(key) % servers setup, going from 3 servers to 4 can remap roughly 75% of your keys, causing a huge spike in cache misses and database traffic.
With consistent hashing, only a small portion of the keyspace moves to the new server, so the rest of your cache stays hot.

title: How TCP, TLS, and HTTP Work Together
summary: Loading an HTTPS website involves a coordinated sequence across several networking layers: DNS resolves the target IP, TCP establishes a reliable connection via a three-way handshake, TLS secures that channel with encryption, and HTTP sends the application payload. On request transmission, TLS encrypts the HTTP request, TCP segments and numbers the packets for ordered delivery, and the server reverses the entire stack upon receipt.
transcript: A lot of people understand that TCP is to make a connection with the server, and then HTTP is to get the data from the server. But when I ask people how TCP and HTTP work together, and what is the sequence, then they usually get confused. Let's make this clear. You open Chrome and type google.com. Even though you never typed http or https, Chrome normally chooses https, which uses port 443. Now, the browser needs Google's IP address before it can connect. So the browser first checks whether it already knows the address, and if not, it performs a DNS lookup to get the IP address. Once the browser has the IP address, it can establish a connection with Google's server. Now, to connect to the server, TCP is the default choice of the browser and the internet. So, let's follow a connection that uses TCP. The browser sends a small packet called SYN to Google's server. Google replies with SYN-ACK, and the browser responds with ACK. This is called the TCP three-way handshake. But what exactly did we achieve? We have established a reliable connection. If some data packets get lost during the travel, TCP can resend them. And TCP makes sure the receiving application gets the bytes in the correct order. However, there is still a big problem. TCP itself does not encrypt the connection. So before we send our HTTP request to the server, we have to secure this connection. And to do that, we have TLS. Let's see what happens. In TLS, your browser sends a message called Client Hello, telling Google which encryption methods it supports, along with some public key information. Google replies with its own public key information and a certificate. The browser checks that the certificate is valid for google.com, and the certificate comes from a trusted authority. Both the browser and server use the exchanged information to calculate encryption keys without ever sending those keys directly over the network. This process is called the TLS handshake. And this is the first step of HTTPS request. Now, let's follow the actual request. The browser creates an HTTP GET request for Google. First, TLS encrypts this request with those encryption keys. Then, TCP takes those encrypted bytes and divides them into smaller pieces. TCP keeps track of the bytes using sequence numbers, so the receiving server can arrange everything back in the correct order. Then, IP adds the source and destination IP addresses, and routers forward these packets toward Google's server. When these packets reach Google's server, the complete process happens in reverse. Data packets can reach Google in wrong order, so TCP puts the received bytes back in the correct order, then TLS decrypts the data, and finally, Google can read the original HTTP GET request that the browser sent. Google then prepares an HTTP response containing the HTML for the homepage. This response goes through TLS, TCP, and IP again, and travels back to your browser. So remember: for a new HTTPS connection over TCP, DNS finds the server's IP address, TCP makes a reliable connection, TLS secures that connection, and HTTP sends the actual request. If this video helped, hit subscribe and follow.
caption:
Interview: How TCP, TLS and HTTP Actually Work Together

When you type a website URL into your browser, several networking protocols must coordinate in a precise order before any webpage can load. First, your browser performs a DNS lookup to translate the domain name into an IP address. Next, it establishes a reliable connection using the TCP three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), which guarantees that dropped packets get resent and data arrives in order. Because standard TCP does not hide your data, the browser immediately initiates a TLS handshake. By verifying the server’s security certificate and generating shared encryption keys, the two machines turn an open connection into a secure HTTPS session.

Once the secure connection is live, your browser formats the actual HTTP GET request. TLS encrypts the message, TCP breaks the data into numbered segments to preserve order, and the IP layer routes those packets across the internet. At the destination, the server reverses the entire pipeline: TCP reassembles the segments, TLS decrypts the payload, and the web server reads the original HTTP request to send back the webpage HTML. Simply put, DNS finds the address, TCP guarantees delivery, TLS locks the connection, and HTTP carries the content.

title: Load Balancing Strategies and Handling Slow Servers
summary: This video breaks down core load balancing strategies and how to handle degraded backends in system design. It contrasts round robin with least connections for handling uneven server performance, explains IP/user hashing for cache locality, and highlights health checks and Layer 4 vs. Layer 7 balancing.
transcript: interview question. users -> load balancer -> server 1, server 2, server 3. Here's a classic interview question. You have three servers behind a load balancer and one of them is slow. How do you stop it from dragging everything down? When one server can't handle all your traffic, you run several. A load balancer sits in front of them. Every request hits it first and it decides which server handles it. The simplest strategy is round robin. Server 1, 2, 3, then back to 1. same cost, same share. Every server gets the same share. That works when every request costs about the same. But our third server is slow. It still gets a third of all requests, it can't finish them in time, and work piles up there. A better strategy is least connections. The balancer sends each new request to the server with the fewest requests still open. The slow server has more open, so it automatically gets fewer new ones. Sometimes a user should always land on the same server to reuse what it has cached. Hashing the user's ID or IP address picks the same server every time. hash(user ID) -> same server. And if a server stops responding entirely, the balancer should notice. Every few seconds, it calls each server's health check. GET /health. A server that fails is taken out of rotation until it recovers. Balancers also work at different layers. A layer 4 balancer only sees IP addresses and ports. A layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request so it can send /api to one group of servers and images to another. The key idea: round robin for even traffic, least connections for uneven work, hashing when users must stick, and health checks always.

author: Arjay McCandless
title: High-Performance Assembly API on a $12 Server
summary: A developer implemented a social media API written in Assembly for a $12/month server challenge, achieving over 17,000 requests per second. The server optimized system performance using Linux io_uring for batched system calls, shared network buffer pools for idle connections, and batched SQLite database transactions.
transcript: I asked developers to write their best code to max out a $12 server and somebody did it in Assembly. The results were insane. For context, the server has one vCPU and 2 gigs of RAM, and it's running a small social media API. I provided the specs for this API. Here's how they implemented it. First, they wrote their own HTTP server, JSON handling, and login verification in Assembly. They used SQLite, which is still written in C. Then they used a Linux interface called io_uring to submit and collect operations in batches. This significantly reduces trips between the application and the operating system, which saves you a ton of speed when you have this many operations going on. Several of our fastest implementations across multiple languages use this same trick. Now, they also optimize around something that you might not think about. Most users spend their time doing nothing. When you're reading something like a long post, your connection is idle. This implementation shares a pool of network buffers, so every single user who may be sitting idle doesn't need their own dedicated buffer at the same time. It also batches database work into transactions, grouping multiple writes together and waiting for the response before sending results out. This implementation was able to support 171,000 simultaneous users, or roughly 17,000 requests per second. Under this load, 99% of requests still finished in under 142 milliseconds, and there was zero errors. Yet, somehow, this was still the second best implementation I got. You can check out all the implementations and detailed breakdowns in my YouTube video tomorrow.
